prompt_sources.name: Example: Finding a Second Solution to a Differential Equation Using Reduction of Order
prompt_sources.problem: Given that $y_1(t) = e^{-t}$ is a solution to the equation $y'' - 3y ' - 4y = 0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution $y_2(t)$ to the equation.
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let $y_{2} = u(t)e^{-t}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =u{e}^{-t} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{-t}-u{e}^{-t} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{-t}-2{u}^{′}{e}^{-t}+u{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}-4y & =0 \\ ({u}^{″}{e}^{-t}-2{u}^{′}{e}^{-t}+u{e}^{-t})-3({u}^{′}{e}^{-t}-u{e}^{-t})-4u{e}^{-t} & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{e}^{-t}-5{u}^{′}{e}^{-t} & =0 \\ {e}^{-t}({u}^{″}-5{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $e^t \neq 0,$ we must have

$$
u'' - 5u' = 0.
$$

Let $w = u'.$ Then our equation becomes a first-order equation,

$$
w' - 5w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w = c_1 e^{5t}.
$$

Now, since since $w = u',$ we have

$$
u' = c_1e^{5t} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u = \dfrac{c_1}{5} e^{5t} + c_2.
$$

Therefore, our expression for $y_2(t) = u e^{-t}$ becomes

$$
y_2(t) = e^{-t}\left( \dfrac{c_1}{5} e^{5t} + c_2 \right).
$$

We can choose any values for $c_1$ and $c_2$ to yield a second solution. For example, if we set $c_1 = 5$ and $c_2 = 0,$ we get

$$
y_2(t) = e^{-t} \cdot e^{5t} = e^{4t}.
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\cdot {x}^{3}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x){x}^{3}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{x}^{3}+3u{x}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{x}^{3}+6{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+6ux.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{3}+6{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+6ux)-x({u}^{′}{x}^{3}+3u{x}^{2})-3u{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}+6{u}^{′}x+6u-{u}^{′}x-3u-3u) & =0 \\ {x}^{4}({u}^{″}x+5{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\cdot {x}^{2}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x){x}^{2}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{x}^{2}+2ux \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{x}^{2}+4{u}^{′}x+2u.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}+4{u}^{′}x+2u)-5x({u}^{′}{x}^{2}+2ux)+8u{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}+4{u}^{′}x+2u-5{u}^{′}x-10u+8u) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}-{u}^{′}x) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}({u}^{″}x-{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{3}\ne 0$ for $x>0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}x-{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}x-w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}x.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}x\,⟹\,u=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}{x}^{2}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{x}^{2}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}(\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}{x}^{2}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}={x}^{4}.
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(t)\cdot {t}^{2}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(t){t}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{t}^{2}+2ut \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u)-3t({u}^{′}{t}^{2}+2ut)+4u{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u-3{u}^{′}t-6u+4u) & =0 \\ {t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+{u}^{′}t) & =0 \\ {t}^{3}({u}^{″}t+{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${t}^{3}\ne 0$ for $t>0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}t+{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}t+w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w=\frac{{c}_{1}}{t}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{t}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}\operatorname{ln} t+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(t)=u{t}^{2}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}({c}_{1}\operatorname{ln} t+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(t)\cdot {t}^{3}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(t){t}^{3}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{t}^{3}+3u{t}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{t}^{3}+6{u}^{′}{t}^{2}+6ut.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{3}+6{u}^{′}{t}^{2}+6ut)-5t({u}^{′}{t}^{3}+3u{t}^{2})+9u{t}^{3} & =0 \\ {t}^{3}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+6{u}^{′}t+6u-5{u}^{′}t-15u+9u) & =0 \\ {t}^{3}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+{u}^{′}t) & =0 \\ {t}^{4}({u}^{″}t+{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${t}^{4}\ne 0$ for $t>0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}t+{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}t+w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w=\frac{{c}_{1}}{t}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{t}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}\operatorname{ln} t+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(t)=u{t}^{3}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(t)={t}^{3}({c}_{1}\operatorname{ln} t+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(t)={t}^{3}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{-2x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2u{e}^{-2x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{-2x}-4{u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}+4u{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{″}{e}^{-2x}-4{u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}+4u{e}^{-2x}-4u{e}^{-2x} & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{e}^{-2x}-4{u}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =0 \\ {e}^{-2x}({u}^{″}-4{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{-2x}\ne 0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}-4{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=4w.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{e}^{4x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{e}^{4x}\,⟹\,u=\frac{{c}_{1}}{4}{e}^{4x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{-2x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}(\frac{{c}_{1}}{4}{e}^{4x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=4$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}\cdot {e}^{4x}={e}^{2x}.
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{2x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2u{e}^{2x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{2x}+4{u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+4u{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}{e}^{2x}+4{u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+4u{e}^{2x})-4({u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2u{e}^{2x})+4u{e}^{2x} & =0 \\ {e}^{2x}({u}^{″}+4{u}^{′}+4u-4{u}^{′}-8u+4u) & =0 \\ {e}^{2x}{u}^{″} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{2x}\ne 0$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=0.
$$

This equation has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{2x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}({c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}\cdot x=x{e}^{2x}.
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)x.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x)x$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}x+u \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′})-2x({u}^{′}x+u)+2ux & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}-2{u}^{′})-2ux+2ux & =0 \\ {x}^{3}{u}^{″} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{3}\ne 0$ for $x>0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
w={c}_{1}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=ux$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=x({c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}.
$$

According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}={e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u) \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u)-2{e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u)+{e}^{x}(u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u-2{u}^{′}-2u+u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}{u}^{″} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=0\,⟹\,w={c}_{1}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}({c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}\cdot x=x{e}^{x}.
$$

prompt_sources.problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation.

solution_sources.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}={e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u) \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u)-{e}^{x}(u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u-u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}+2w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{e}^{-2x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{e}^{-2x}\,⟹\,u=-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}{e}^{-2x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}(-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}{e}^{-2x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-2$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{-2x}={e}^{-x}.
$$

prompt_sources.problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-6y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation.

solution_sources.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{3x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{3x}+6{u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+9u{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}{e}^{3x}+6{u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+9u{e}^{3x})-({u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x})-6u{e}^{3x} & =0 \\ {e}^{3x}({u}^{″}+6{u}^{′}+9u-{u}^{′}-3u-6u) & =0 \\ {e}^{3x}({u}^{″}+5{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{3x}\ne 0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}+5{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}+5w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{e}^{-5x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{e}^{-5x}\,⟹\,u=-\frac{{c}_{1}}{5}{e}^{-5x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{3x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}(-\frac{{c}_{1}}{5}{e}^{-5x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-5$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}\cdot {e}^{-5x}={e}^{-2x}.
$$

prompt_sources.problem: The function ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation $x{y}^{″}-(x+1){y}^{′}+y=0$ for $x>0.$ Use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation.

solution_sources.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\cdot {e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x({u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})-(x+1)({u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})+u{e}^{x} & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux)-{e}^{x}{u}^{′}(x+1)-{e}^{x}u(x+1)+{e}^{x}u & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux-{u}^{′}(x+1)-u(x+1)+u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(2x-x-1)+u(x-x-1+1)) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}x+w(x-1)=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}\,⟹\,u=-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}(-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=(1+x).
$$

prompt_sources.problem:
The function $y_1(x) = e^{3x}$ is a solution to the equation $y'' - 6y' + 9y = 0.$ If $y_{2} = u(x) y_1(x)$ is a second solution of the equation, then which of the following equations must be satisfied by $u(x)?$

I. $u''=0$

II. $e^{3x}u'' + u=0$

III. $u''-u=0$
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
We're given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =u(x){y}_{1}(x) \\  & =u(x){e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =u{e}^{3x} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{3x}+6{u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+9u{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}-6{y}^{′}+9y & =0 \\ ({u}^{″}{e}^{3x}+6{u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+9u{e}^{3x})-6({u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x})+9u{e}^{3x} & =0 \\ {e}^{3x}({u}^{″}+6{u}^{′}+9u-6{u}^{′}-18u+9u) & =0 \\ {e}^{3x}{u}^{″} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $e^{3x} \neq 0,$ we must have

$$
u'' = 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

prompt_sources.problem: The function ${y}_{1}(x)=x$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{2}{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}-5y=0$ for $x>0.$ If ${y}_{2}=u(x){y}_{1}(x)$ is a second solution of the equation, then which of the following equations must be satisfied by $u(x)?$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=u(x){y}_{1}(x)=ux.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=ux$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}x+u \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′})+5x({u}^{′}x+u)-5ux & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{x}^{3}+2{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+5{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+5ux-5ux & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{x}^{3}+7{u}^{′}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({u}^{″}x+7{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{2}\ne 0$ for $x>0,$ we must have

$$
x{u}^{″}+7{u}^{′}=0.
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(t)=u(t){y}_{1}(t)=u{e}^{-3t}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u{e}^{-3t}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{-3t}-3u{e}^{-3t} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{-3t}-6{u}^{′}{e}^{-6t}+9u{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}{e}^{-3t}-6{u}^{′}{e}^{-6t}+9u{e}^{-3t})+2({u}^{′}{e}^{-3t}-3u{e}^{-3t})-3u{e}^{-3t} & =0 \\ {e}^{-3t}({u}^{″}-6{u}^{′}+9u+2{u}^{′}-6u-3u) & =0 \\ {e}^{-3t}({u}^{″}-4{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{-3t}\ne 0$ for all $t,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}-4{u}^{′}=0.
$$

We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=u(x){y}_{1}(x)=u\operatorname{cos} x.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u\operatorname{cos} x$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}\operatorname{cos} x-u\operatorname{sin} x \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}\operatorname{cos} x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin} x-u\operatorname{cos} x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}\operatorname{cos} x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin} x-u\operatorname{cos} x)+u\operatorname{cos} x & =0 \\ {u}^{″}\operatorname{cos} x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin} x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(t)=u(t){y}_{1}(t)=u{t}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u{t}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{t}^{2}+2ut \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u)-2u{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u-2u) & =0 \\ {t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t) & =0 \\ {t}^{3}({u}^{″}t+4{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${t}^{3}\ne 0$ for $t>0,$ we must have

$$
t{u}^{″}+4{u}^{′}=0.
$$

$$
{y}_{2}(t)=u(t){y}_{1}(t)=u\operatorname{sin} 2t.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u\operatorname{sin} 2t$ with respect to $t$ gives

\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}\operatorname{sin} 2t+2u\operatorname{cos} 2t \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}\operatorname{sin} 2t+4{u}^{′}\operatorname{cos} 2t-4u\operatorname{sin} 2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}\operatorname{sin} 2t+4{u}^{′}\operatorname{cos} 2t-4u\operatorname{sin} 2t)+4u\operatorname{sin} 2t & =0 \\ {u}^{″}\operatorname{sin} 2t+4{u}^{′}\operatorname{cos} 2t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
